findings.claim: `source_mutated`'s undo is `git checkout HEAD -- <file>`, which silently discards *any* uncommitted change to that file, not just the mutation it applied — and its own docstring (line 394) justifies this by claiming `committed` guarantees the tree is already committed before any gate runs. That guarantee is not actually enforced: in `session.py`, `commit_dirty` is only invoked on the `AgentFailed`/crash paths (session.py:1452-1455, 1573-1576), never after an ordinary successful repair turn, and `committed_gate` itself is computed (session.py:1049) only *after* `declared = run_suite(...)` (session.py:1008) has already run `witness`/`source_mutated` and reverted with `git checkout HEAD --`. If the mutant's target file happens to hold uncommitted implementer edits when a repair attempt's gate suite runs — plausible, since a criterion's mutant typically names the very source file the task is editing — that work is destroyed by the checkout before `committed_gate` even samples `dirty_paths`, and because the checkout erases the evidence, `committed` can then report `pass` (clean) even though real work was just lost. No existing test exercises a dirty target file at mutation time (`tests/test_worktree.py`'s fixtures always commit and stay clean before calling `source_mutated`), so nothing here would catch it, and the failure mode is currently dormant only because no spec in this repo yet declares a mutant.

`_write_file` (the call that actually truncates and rewrites `mutant.file` via `> path` inside the container) runs before the `try/finally` that restores from `HEAD`, unlike `source_reverted` a few lines above it (341-345) which wraps its own mutating call in the same `try` that guarantees a restore. If the write's shell pipeline opens/truncates the destination and then fails partway (disk pressure, the exec losing the connection after the redirect took effect, etc.), `_write_file` raises before `source_mutated` ever reaches `yield None`, so `witness_gate`'s `applied` flag (witness.py lines 78-85, 142-154) is still `False` and the failure is reported as "could not apply {file}'s mutant" — the message that means nothing was touched — when the file may in fact be left mutated with no restore attempted. witness.py's own docstring names this exact case as the one obligation `host_mutator` satisfies for free but a 'container exec that applies the edit and then loses the connection' does not, and calls a mutated tree reported this way 'the silent dirty tree this gate exists to refuse.' The docstring on `source_mutated` (403-405) claims 'any other failure to apply... raises... never a verdict on the claim' but does not honor the stronger invariant witness.py documents: a raise from entry must mean nothing changed. The gates cannot see this because it requires the write to fail after partially succeeding, a case none of the added tests exercise (they only fail `_read_file` or the undo `_git checkout`, never `_write_file` itself).

Every mutant used against `source_mutated` across this file (lines 1049, 1065, 1092, 1099, 1112) has `find`/`replace` text drawn only from identifiers, digits and punctuation like `:`/`<`/`=` — none contains a quote, backslash, or `$`/backtick. `worktree._write_file`'s own docstring names quotes and backslashes by name as exactly what base64-encoding the content exists to make safe for the `printf … | base64 -d` shell line. Replacing `_write_file`'s body with `script = f"printf '%s' '{content}' > {shlex.quote(path)}"` (dropping the base64 round trip and interpolating `content` raw inside a naive single-quoted shell string) would pass every test in this file unchanged, since no fixture's mutated content contains a `'`, yet it would corrupt or fail on any real Python source line containing a string literal (`raise ValueError("bad")`, `x = 'y'`), which is the ordinary shape of the source this mutator is meant to edit. No test would catch that regression.
